subject: frontend
question: Does calling add('Buy milk') make the new todo appear on screen?
ai_claim: Yes. The todo is pushed into the array and setTodos is called, which triggers a re-render showing it.

ai_solution.text: todos.push adds the text to the array.
setTodos(todos) passes the updated array to React.
Calling a state setter always re-renders the component.

failure.misconception: Mutating state and passing the same reference
failure.explanation: React compares the new state with the old using Object.is. push mutates the existing array, so setTodos receives the same reference, React sees no change and bails out of re-rendering. The todo does not appear (until something else causes a render). Create a new array: setTodos([...todos, text]).
failure.why_convincing: The array does contain the new item, and 'set state causes a render' is a common rule of thumb.

canonical_solution: No: the same array reference is passed, so React skips the re-render. Use setTodos(prev => [...prev, text]).

valid_evidence.summary: Clicking add shows no change; the list updates only when another state change forces a render.

counterexamples: The list stays the same after add('Buy milk').

hints.text: Check how React decides whether state changed.
Step 3 says a setter call always re-renders.
React compares state by reference (Object.is); mutation keeps the same reference.
Compare the array passed to setTodos with the current state.
Step 3 is wrong: the same reference means no re-render. Create a new array.

debrief: React state must be treated as immutable: change it by replacing it. Mutation both skips renders and breaks features that depend on previous values (memoisation, concurrent rendering, dev tools).

subject: frontend
question: After sorting, does the text the user typed stay with the same item?
ai_claim: Yes. Keys are the stable item ids, so React moves each <li> - and its input's typed text - with its item.

ai_solution.text: React matches elements between renders by key.
Each item's key is its id, which does not change when sorting.
React therefore reorders the existing DOM nodes instead of reusing them by position.
The typed text moves with its item.

canonical_solution: Correct. With stable keys, React preserves each element's identity and internal state across reorders. With index keys, the typed text would stay at the same position and appear under a different item.

valid_evidence.summary: Type into the second input, sort: the text follows its item to its new position.
With key={index}, the typed text stays in the second row, now showing a different item.

hints.text: Check how React identifies list items between renders.
Step 2 depends on the key staying the same when the order changes.
Keys give elements identity; stable ids keep that identity across reorders.
Compare key={item.id} with key={index} after sorting.
This solution is correct. Stable id keys make React move each item with its state. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Keys are identity, not just a warning suppressor. Index keys are fine only for lists that never reorder, insert or delete in the middle. The claim uses stable ids and explains why they matter.

subject: frontend
question: Starting from 0, does one click show 2?
ai_claim: Yes. Each updater receives the latest pending state, so the first update makes 1 and the second makes 2.

ai_solution.text: Both setCount calls are queued during the click handler.
React applies queued updaters in order.
The first receives 0 and returns 1; the second receives 1 and returns 2.

canonical_solution: Correct. Updater functions chain on the pending state. (setCount(count + 1) twice would show 1, because both calls use the same stale count.)

valid_evidence.summary: With setCount(count + 1) twice, one click shows 1.

hints.text: Check what each updater function receives.
Step 3 chains the two updates.
Updater functions receive the most recent pending state, not the value from the render.
Apply the two updaters in order starting from 0.
This solution is correct. The updaters chain, 0 -> 1 -> 2. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: When new state depends on old state, use the updater form. It avoids the stale values that closures capture, the same issue behind stale state in intervals and effects.

subject: frontend
question: Does the tracking effect run only when a different user is shown, and not on every re-render of the parent?
ai_claim: Yes. The effect depends on user, so it runs only when the user changes, not on unrelated re-renders.

ai_solution.text: useEffect re-runs when a dependency changes.
Re-rendering the parent does not change which user is shown.
So the effect runs only when a different user is shown.

missing_information: How the parent creates the user prop. Dependencies are compared by reference: if the parent builds a new object each render (user={{ id, name }}) the effect runs on every parent render; if it passes a stable object (from state or memoised), it runs only when the user changes.
resolving_scenarios: The parent passes user from useState or a cache: the reference is stable and the effect runs only when the user changes.
The parent renders <Profile user={{ id: u.id, name: u.name }} />: a new object each render, so the effect runs on every render.
canonical_solution: It depends on the parent, which is not shown. Step 3 assumes the same user means the same reference. Depending on [user.id] would make the answer 'yes' either way.

valid_evidence.summary: If the parent passes user={{ ...u }}, each render creates a new object and the effect runs again.

counterexamples: An inline object prop re-triggers the effect on every parent render.

hints.text: Check how React compares dependencies.
Step 3 assumes an unchanged user is the same object.
Dependencies are compared with Object.is, so a new object with the same content counts as a change.
Consider a parent that writes user={{ id: 1, name: 'Asha' }}.
Step 3 assumes a stable reference. A stable user runs it once; an inline object runs it every render. It cannot be decided.

repair: Depend on the primitive that matters: `[user.id]`.
debrief: Effect dependencies are compared by reference, so whether an effect re-runs can depend on code in another component. Depend on primitive values (ids) rather than objects when you can.
